# A1 · Interfaces and State Machine {.unnumbered}

Step A1 of the [Implementation Plan](00-4-structure-and-verification.qmd#implementation-plan) builds the frame of the new firmware: the interfaces, the state machine, the test doubles and the first tests. No module is wired yet: the only hardware needed is the ESP32 board and its USB cable.

The step is split into three chapters:

1. **Interfaces and State Machine** (this chapter): the project layout, the interfaces, and the core logic.
2. [Tests](01-2-tests.qmd): the test doubles, and the automatic tests of the core on the computer.
3. [Walking Skeleton](01-3-walking-skeleton.qmd): the same state machine running on the board, with *skeleton adapters* that stand in for the modules.

The following steps replace the skeleton adapters one by one with real ones (DS3231 in A2, BME280 and SD card in A3, Wi-Fi in A4, access point in A5), without changing the state machine.

> **Ready-to-use project:** The complete code of step A1 is available in the repository here: [`firmware/paws`](https://github.com/wg1d/personal-autonomous-weather-station/tree/v0.2.0/firmware/paws)

> **API reference:** Every class and function of the firmware is documented in the code, with [Doxygen](https://www.doxygen.nl/) comments. The generated documentation is published with this book: [firmware API](../../../api/index.html)

## Project Layout

The PoC had one folder per sketch. From now on, the firmware is a single PlatformIO project, which grows at each step:

```text
firmware/paws/
├── platformio.ini
├── lib/
│   ├── ports/            # interfaces and the data they exchange
│   │   ├── Record.h
│   │   ├── IClock.h, ISensor.h, IStorage.h
│   │   ├── INetwork.h, IPower.h, IMaintenance.h
│   │   └── ILog.h
│   └── core/             # decision logic, no Arduino
│       ├── Config.h
│       ├── Rules.h, Rules.cpp
│       ├── Transitions.h, Transitions.cpp
│       └── StateMachine.h, StateMachine.cpp
├── src/
│   ├── adapters/         # skeleton adapters in this step
│   └── main.cpp
└── test/
    ├── doubles/          # test doubles
    ├── test_rules/       # unit tests of the rules
    ├── test_transitions/ # unit tests of the transitions
    └── test_scenarios/   # scenario tests
```

PlatformIO treats each folder of `lib/` as a library, compiled for any environment that includes one of its headers. `src/` is only compiled for the board, and each `test_*` folder of `test/` is a separate test program.

The project has two environments:

```{.ini include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/platformio.ini"}
```

- `esp32` builds the firmware, as in the PoC.
- `native` builds `lib/` and `test/` with the computer's compiler (`g++`), and runs the tests with [Unity](https://github.com/ThrowTheSwitch/Unity). `-std=gnu++11` selects the same version of C++ as the Arduino core of the board, so that the tests compile the code exactly as the board does. `-Wall -Wextra` enable the compiler warnings, and `-I test/doubles` lets every test include the test doubles.

## The Data

The `lib/ports` folder contains what the core needs from the outside world, in its own terms. It holds two kinds of files, with different roles:

- An **interface** describes a *service*: functions that the core can call, without saying how they work. Each interface has several implementations. For the clock: `SystemClock` on the board in this step, `Ds3231Clock` from step A2, and `FakeClock` in the tests. By convention, the name of an interface starts with `I`.
- A **data structure** describes *values*: a timestamp, a validity flag, measurements. It has no functions to implement, and a single definition, used as is by the core, the adapters and the tests. It is what travels through the interfaces: the core fills a `Record`, then gives it to `IStorage::append()`. Its name has no `I`.

The data is a single file for now, `Record.h`. It defines a `Measurement` (one reading of all the sensors) and a `Record`: the [row](00-1-requirements.qmd) created at each wake-up, which the storage writes as one line of the CSV file:

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/lib/ports/Record.h"}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## C++: `#pragma once`, `uint32_t`, `struct` and default values

- **`#pragma once`** tells the compiler to read this header only once per source file, even when several headers include it. Without it, the same `struct` would be defined twice, which is an error. The older form, an `#ifndef`/`#define`/`#endif` *include guard*, does the same thing in three lines; `#pragma once` is shorter and supported by every compiler we use.
- **`uint32_t`** is an unsigned integer of exactly 32 bits, on the ESP32 as on the computer. A plain `int` or `long` can have a different size on each, and the tests must compute exactly what the board computes. 32 bits hold Unix times until the year 2106.
- **`struct`** and `class` are almost the same in C++; the only difference is that the members of a `struct` are public by default. By convention, we use `struct` for plain data (fields only) and `class` for objects with behavior.
- **`= NAN`, `= 0`** give each field a default value. A new `Measurement` therefore starts with every value "missing", and a sensor only fills what it could read.
:::

A value that could not be measured is `NAN` (*Not a Number*), a special floating-point value meaning "no value". It follows the "missing values" rule of the [Design Invariants](00-1-requirements.qmd#design-invariants): the storage will write it as an empty field, never as a fake number such as `0` or `-999`.

## The Interfaces

There is one interface per service. As in the [Structure and Verification](00-4-structure-and-verification.qmd#what-an-interface-looks-like) chapter, each one only declares functions (*pure virtual* functions, marked `= 0`).

Each interface only declares what step A1 uses; the next steps add functions when they need them.

### IClock

The clock gives the core the time, and wakes the station up at the right moment. The core uses it to:

- timestamp each row (`now()`), and flag the row when the time is not reliable (`isValid()`, F6 · Flag unreliable time);
- correct the time after an NTP sync (`setTime()`), and remember when it was done (`lastSetTime()`), to know when the next sync is due (F4 · Daily time sync);
- program the next measurement on the 15-minute grid (`setAlarm()`).

This is the interface presented in the [Structure and Verification](00-4-structure-and-verification.qmd#what-an-interface-looks-like) chapter, with one detail: `setAlarm()` returns `false` when no alarm could be programmed, for example when the RTC does not answer. The core then knows that the RTC alarm will not wake the station up, and relies on the ESP32 safety timer instead, so that the station never sleeps forever (N2 · Always wake up again).

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/lib/ports/IClock.h"}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## C++: `virtual`, `= 0` and the virtual destructor

- **`virtual`** means that the function called is chosen *at run time*, according to the real object: when the state machine calls `clock.now()`, it runs `SystemClock::now()` on the board in this step, and `FakeClock::now()` in the tests.
- **`= 0`** makes the function *pure virtual*: the interface declares it without writing it, and every class that implements the interface must write it. A class with a pure virtual function cannot be created on its own.
- **`virtual ~IClock() = default;`** is the destructor, called when an object is destroyed. Making it `virtual` guarantees that destroying an object through its interface also runs the destructor of the real class. We never do it in this firmware, but it is the rule for any class meant to be used through an interface, and it costs nothing. `= default` asks the compiler to write the (empty) destructor.

Another way to swap implementations would be *templates*, resolved at compile time. Virtual functions are simpler to read and to explain, and their cost (one indirect call) is negligible at a few calls per wake-up.
:::

### ISensor

The sensors give the core the values of a row. A single function reads all of them at once and returns a `Measurement`. Adding a sensor (N5 · Extensibility) adds a field to `Measurement`, not a function here.

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/lib/ports/ISensor.h"}
```

### IStorage

The storage keeps every row on the SD card, the source of truth of the station. In this step, it only appends rows; reading the rows after the upload cursor comes with the upload, in step A4.

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/lib/ports/IStorage.h"}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## C++: `const Record&`

`append(const Record& record)` receives the row *by reference* (`&`): the function works on the caller's row instead of a copy, which avoids copying the whole structure. `const` promises that the function will not modify it. This is the usual way to pass a structure that is only read.
:::

### INetwork

The network lets the core reach the home Wi-Fi, the server and NTP. In this step, it opens and closes the connection, and reads the NTP time. `fetchTime()` is only called while connected: the daily sync reuses the upload connection (F4 · Daily time sync). Sending the rows comes in step A4.

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/lib/ports/INetwork.h"}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## C++: an output parameter, `uint32_t& unixTime`

`fetchTime()` must return two things: whether NTP answered, and the time. It returns the first one (`bool`), and writes the second one into a variable of the caller, passed by reference without `const`. Recent C++ versions offer `std::optional` for this, but it does not exist in C++11, the version of the Arduino core.
:::

### IPower

The power management tells the core why the station woke up, and puts it back to deep sleep. It defines the four wake-up causes, and the `SleepPlan`: the list of wake-up sources to arm before sleeping, as decided by the core.

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/lib/ports/IPower.h"}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## C++: `enum class`

An `enum class` lists named values, here the wake-up causes. Compared to a plain `enum`, the names must be written with their type (`WakeCause::Button`, not just `Button`), so two enumerations can use the same name without conflict, and a value cannot be mixed up with an integer by mistake.
:::

### IMaintenance

The maintenance mode (F5) lets someone download or delete the data from a phone, through an access point and a web page. The core only starts the session and waits for its end: the Wi-Fi and the web server stay hidden behind this interface.

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/lib/ports/IMaintenance.h"}
```

### ILog

The log lets someone follow the path of a wake-up: the state machine reports each state it enters. On the board, the names are printed on the serial port; in the tests, they are kept, so that a test can check the path.

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/lib/ports/ILog.h"}
```

## The Core

### Configuration

All the settings of the core are grouped in one structure. Its default values are those of the Phase 4 design; `main.cpp` and the tests can change them.

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/lib/core/Config.h"}
```

### The rules

The conditions of the transitions are *pure functions*: their result only depends on their arguments, and they have no side effect (no hardware access, no global variable). This is what makes them easy to test.

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/lib/core/Rules.h"}
```

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/lib/core/Rules.cpp"}
```

Two details matter here:

- `isUploadNeeded()` tests the **slot** of the measurement, not its exact time. The firmware reads the clock a few seconds after the alarm, so testing `t % 3600 == 0` would almost never be true. With the slot, a measurement at `14:00:03`, or at `14:01:00` after a wake-up by the safety timer, triggers the hourly upload.
- `uint32_t` is an *unsigned* integer: it cannot be negative. Subtracting a larger number from a smaller one "wraps around" and gives a very large number. `isSyncNeeded()` relies on it: if the clock went backwards, the age of the last sync looks huge, and a sync is requested.

### The transitions

A state machine does two different things at each step: it does the *work* of the current state (read the sensors, store the row...), then it chooses the *next state*. We keep them apart. The work is done by the state machine (next section), and the choice of the next state is a single pure function, `nextState()`.

This choice depends on **conditions**: the "Condition" column of the [transitions table](00-2-behavior.qmd#state-machine) in the Behavior chapter. There are four of them: whether the button woke the station up, whether an upload is needed, whether the Wi-Fi is connected, and whether a sync is needed. They are grouped in a `Conditions` structure. Each one is set by the state that can know it: BOOT reads the wake-up cause, STORE computes whether an upload is needed, and UPLOAD tries to connect and computes whether a sync is needed. `nextState()` only reads them.

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/lib/core/Transitions.h"}
```

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/lib/core/Transitions.cpp"}
```

Each `case` corresponds to one or two rows of the [transitions table](00-2-behavior.qmd#state-machine) of the Behavior chapter: all the transitions of the station are in this one function, and can be checked against the table line by line.

### The state machine

The state machine does the work of each state, and asks `nextState()` where to go next. Its header declares everything it needs:

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/lib/core/StateMachine.h"}
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## C++: references in `Ports`

`Ports` holds *references* (`IClock&`) rather than pointers (`IClock*`). A reference must be given when the object is created, and can never be null: the machine cannot be built with a missing interface, and never has to check for one. The objects themselves are created once, by `main.cpp` or by the test, and live as long as the machine.
:::

From top to bottom:

- **`Ports`** groups the seven interfaces the machine works with. It is only a bundle of references, so that the constructor takes one argument instead of seven. On the board, `main.cpp` fills it with the hardware adapters; in the tests, with the test doubles. The machine never knows which ones it uses.
- **The constructor** receives the settings (`Config`) and the `Ports`, and keeps them.
- **`run()`** is the only public function: it runs one wake-up, from BOOT to SLEEP.
- **The private part** contains `doWork()`, which calls the `on...()` function of a state, and the `on...()` functions themselves: the work of each state. It ends with the variables that the states of one wake-up pass to each other: the conditions read by `nextState()`, whether the clock is valid, the row filled by MEASURE and stored by STORE, and the sleep plan prepared by SCHEDULE for SLEEP.

The implementation follows:

```{.cpp include="../../../_versions/v0.2.0/firmware/paws/lib/core/StateMachine.cpp"}
```

`run()` repeats the usual cycle of a state machine, until `SLEEP`. Before each cycle, the name of the current state is reported to the log.

1. **Actions of the current state**: `doWork()` calls the matching `on...()` function. These actions also read the inputs of the state (the wake-up cause in BOOT, the result of the connection in UPLOAD...) and set the matching conditions.
2. **Evolution**: `nextState()` chooses the next state from the conditions.
3. **Actions on transitions**: there are none in this machine; all the actions belong to the states.
4. **The next state becomes the current state**, and the cycle starts again.

The core is complete, but nothing has run yet. The [next chapter](01-2-tests.qmd) checks it on the computer.
